tasks.description: Set up the foundational structure and build configuration for an Elm 0.19 Single Page Application integrated with Vite and Phoenix backend, including project directories, Elm package configuration, and development server with hot reload.
tasks.details:
Begin by initializing the Elm project structure. Create the following directories at the root level: `src/` for Elm source files, `tests/` for test files, and `public/` for static assets. Initialize an Elm project using `elm init`, which will generate `elm.json`. Update `elm.json` to include required packages: add `elm/browser` for browser interactions, `elm/http` for HTTP requests, and `elm/json` for JSON handling. Ensure Elm version is set to 0.19.

Next, integrate Vite for build tooling. Install Vite and esbuild as dependencies (e.g., via npm or yarn). Configure Vite in `vite.config.js` to handle Elm compilation: use the `vite-plugin-elm` plugin to compile Elm files, and set up bundling to include `phoenix.js` for Phoenix integration. Configure the output to serve static files from the `public/` directory.

For Phoenix integration, ensure the Phoenix application is set up to serve static files from the build output directory (typically `dist/` or similar). Update Phoenix's `endpoint.ex` to serve static files from the Elm build directory, and configure routes to handle SPA routing (e.g., fallback to `index.html` for client-side routing).

Set up the development server with hot reload: Configure Vite's dev server to proxy API requests to the Phoenix backend (running on a different port, e.g., 4000). Enable hot module replacement for Elm files using the plugin. Add scripts in `package.json` for development (e.g., `vite dev`) and build (e.g., `vite build`).

Considerations: Ensure compatibility between Elm 0.19 and Vite/esbuild. Handle CORS if the dev server proxies to Phoenix. For production, ensure the build process minifies and optimizes the bundle. If using a monorepo, ensure paths are correctly configured.
tasks.testStrategy: Verify the project structure by checking that `src/`, `tests/`, and `public/` directories exist and are populated appropriately (e.g., a basic Elm file in `src/Main.elm`). Run `elm make` to ensure `elm.json` is valid and packages are installed without errors. Test Vite integration by running the dev server (`npm run dev` or equivalent) and confirming that Elm files compile successfully, with hot reload working (edit an Elm file and observe changes in the browser without full reload). Check Phoenix static file serving by building the project (`npm run build`) and verifying that the Phoenix server serves the bundled files correctly (e.g., access the app at the Phoenix port and confirm Elm SPA loads). Test API proxying by making a request from the Elm app to the Phoenix backend and ensuring it resolves without CORS errors. Run any initial tests in the `tests/` directory to confirm the testing setup.

tasks.description: Implement comprehensive security measures for the Elm web client, including secure session handling with Guardian tokens, CSRF protection, XSS prevention, CSP headers, rate limiting, secure WebSocket validation, token refresh, session timeout, encrypted local storage, audit logging, clickjacking protection, and documentation of best practices.

Build a token refresh mechanism in the auth state from Task 5, automatically retrying failed requests with refreshed tokens via subscriptions and update functions. Handle session timeout by monitoring token expiry in the state management module, triggering logout and redirect on timeout. Add secure local storage encryption for sensitive data (e.g., user preferences) using Elm's ports to interface with JavaScript's localStorage with encryption (e.g., using crypto-js via JS interop). Implement security audit logging by extending the API client to log security events (e.g., failed logins, token refreshes) to a backend endpoint. Prevent clickjacking by adding X-Frame-Options headers in the Vite config and using Elm's Html to include frame-busting scripts if necessary. Finally, document security best practices in a README or dedicated doc, covering topics like input validation, secure coding in Elm, and integration with Phoenix backend security.

Test client-side rate limiting by rapidly submitting forms and verifying throttling messages appear. Confirm token refresh by expiring tokens manually and observing automatic retries in API calls. Test session timeout by setting short expiry times and verifying logout triggers. For encrypted local storage, inspect localStorage via dev tools to ensure data is encrypted and decryptable only with keys. tasks.title: Elm Web Client: Performance Optimization & Bundle Analysis
tasks.description: Optimize the Elm web client for production performance by implementing Elm compilation optimizations, code splitting, lazy loading, virtual scrolling, WebSocket enhancements, message batching, performance monitoring, bundle analysis, CSS optimizations, performance budgets, and Lighthouse CI integration.
tasks.details: Begin by configuring Elm compilation for production using the --optimize flag in the build process, which enables dead code elimination, function inlining, and other optimizations to reduce bundle size and improve runtime performance. Implement code splitting for large features by using Elm's lazy loading capabilities with Browser.application or custom ports to dynamically load modules like the bridge panel or advanced message views, ensuring that initial bundle size remains small and subsequent loads are efficient. Create lazy loading for the bridge panel by wrapping it in a lazy view that loads on demand when the user interacts with the bridge insights toggle, integrating with the layout state from Task 14. Build virtual scrolling for long message lists by implementing a custom Elm component that renders only visible items (e.g., using a viewport calculation with Html.lazy and subscriptions for scroll events), calculating item heights dynamically and maintaining scroll position to handle thousands of messages without performance degradation. Optimize WebSocket event handling by batching incoming channel messages in the JavaScript adapter from Task 3, using a debounced port to send batched updates to Elm, reducing frequent re-renders. Implement message batching for bulk operations by modifying the API client in Task 4 to support batch endpoints for sending multiple messages or updates in a single HTTP request, with retry logic and error handling. Add performance monitoring hooks by integrating Elm's Time.every or custom ports to track metrics like render times, WebSocket latency, and API response times, logging them via ports to a monitoring service. Build bundle size analysis tooling by adding webpack-bundle-analyzer or similar to the build pipeline, generating reports on module sizes and dependencies to identify optimization opportunities. Optimize CSS delivery by inlining critical CSS (above-the-fold styles for the dashboard layout from Task 14) using a tool like critical or manual extraction, and loading non-critical CSS asynchronously. Create performance budgets by defining thresholds in the build configuration (e.g., max bundle size 2MB, max Lighthouse scores 90+), failing builds that exceed them. Add Lighthouse CI integration by configuring GitHub Actions or similar to run Lighthouse audits on pull requests, generating reports and blocking merges on score regressions. Ensure all optimizations maintain compatibility with existing features like real-time updates from Task 6, authentication from Task 2, and responsive design from Task 14, and consider accessibility impacts to avoid regressions with Task 15.
tasks.testStrategy: Verify Elm compilation optimizations by comparing build outputs with and without the --optimize flag, confirming reduced bundle size and improved load times using browser network tools or Lighthouse audits. Test code splitting by inspecting the initial bundle size and monitoring network requests during lazy loading of features like the bridge panel, ensuring dynamic imports load only when triggered. Confirm lazy loading for the bridge panel by toggling the panel in the UI and checking that the component loads asynchronously without blocking the main thread, using browser dev tools to observe network and performance timelines. Validate virtual scrolling for message lists by populating a thread with thousands of messages, scrolling rapidly, and verifying smooth performance with no lag or memory leaks, using Elm's debugger or browser profiler to check render counts and memory usage. Assess WebSocket optimization by simulating high-frequency channel events and monitoring Elm's update frequency, ensuring batched updates reduce re-renders via console logs or performance traces. Test message batching by performing bulk operations (e.g., sending multiple messages) and confirming single HTTP requests via network logs, with error scenarios triggering retries. Check performance monitoring hooks by triggering various app actions and verifying metrics are logged correctly via ports, integrating with a test monitoring endpoint. Evaluate bundle analysis tooling by running the build and reviewing generated reports for module sizes, identifying and addressing any unexpectedly large dependencies. Confirm CSS optimization by auditing page load with tools like PageSpeed Insights, ensuring critical CSS is inlined and non-critical loads asynchronously without flash of unstyled content. Validate performance budgets by running builds and ensuring they pass/fail based on defined thresholds, using CI logs. Test Lighthouse CI integration by creating a pull request, confirming automated audits run, scores meet budgets, and reports are generated without false positives.

tasks.title: Elm Web Client: Telemetry & Analytics Integration
tasks.description: Integrate telemetry and analytics into the Elm web client to emit Phoenix telemetry events for thread subscriptions and unsubscriptions, capture key user interactions such as login success/failure and message sends, and implement a configurable analytics provider with performance metrics, error tracking, and privacy-respecting user engagement metrics.
tasks.details: Begin by defining Elm types for telemetry events, such as union types for Event (e.g., ThreadSubscribed { threadId : String }, ThreadUnsubscribed { threadId : String }, LoginSuccess { userId : String }, LoginFailure { reason : String }, MessageSent { threadId : String, messageId : String }, BridgeRetry { bridgeId : String, attempt : Int }, PageLoad { duration : Float }, FirstMessageSent { duration : Float }, ChannelConnection { duration : Float }, ErrorOccurred { context : String, error : String }, UserEngaged { action : String }). Ensure these types are privacy-respecting by excluding any personally identifiable information (PII) like email addresses or full names, using anonymized IDs instead. Integrate with the Phoenix Channels JavaScript interop from Task 3 by extending the phoenixAdapter.js to emit telemetry events via ports, for example, adding outgoing ports like `emitTelemetry : Event -> Cmd msg` and handling them in JavaScript to send events to Phoenix telemetry (e.g., using Phoenix's telemetry API or custom logging). For user interactions, hook into the authentication flow from Task 2 to emit LoginSuccess/LoginFailure events on auth state changes in the update function. For message sends, integrate with the state management from Task 5 to emit MessageSent events when messages are successfully sent via the REST API client from Task 4. For thread subscriptions/unsubscriptions, extend the thread list view from Task 6 to emit events when subscribing/unsubscribing to channels. Build a lightweight analytics adapter module in Elm, starting with a console logging implementation for development (e.g., a DevAnalytics module that logs events to console.log). Create a configurable AnalyticsProvider interface using Elm's extensible records or union types, allowing for different providers (e.g., Console, ProductionApi), with a default dev provider that logs to console and a prod provider that can be configured via environment variables to send data to an external analytics service via HTTP requests using the API client. Implement performance metrics by using Browser.Events and Time modules to track page load times (e.g., on app initialization), first message sent (timestamp from state), and channel connection times (from Task 3's reconnection logic). Add error tracking by integrating with the API client's error handling in Task 4 to emit ErrorOccurred events with context (e.g., API endpoint, error type). For user engagement metrics, track actions like thread switches or bridge panel opens by emitting UserEngaged events in relevant update functions. Ensure all tracking is opt-in or configurable, with no automatic PII collection, and document all event types, fields, and emission points in a stakeholder-facing document (e.g., a Markdown file in the repo). Consider using Elm's Task and Cmd for asynchronous telemetry emission to avoid blocking the UI.
tasks.testStrategy: Verify telemetry event emission by running the Elm app in development mode and using browser console to check for logged events during key interactions: log in successfully and confirm LoginSuccess event with anonymized userId; attempt invalid login and check LoginFailure; send a message and verify MessageSent with threadId and messageId; subscribe/unsubscribe to a thread and inspect ThreadSubscribed/Unsubscribed events. Test performance metrics by monitoring console logs on app load for PageLoad duration, after sending first message for FirstMessageSent, and on channel connection for ChannelConnection. Simulate errors (e.g., network failure in API calls) and confirm ErrorOccurred events with context. For user engagement, perform actions like switching threads and check UserEngaged events. Switch to production config and verify events are sent via HTTP (mock the endpoint if needed) instead of console. Use elm-test to unit test event type definitions and analytics adapter functions, ensuring no PII is included (e.g., fuzz test event creation with random data). Document and review analytics events with stakeholders to confirm completeness and privacy compliance.

tasks.title: Elm Web Client: E2EE Preparation & Message Rendering Abstraction
tasks.description: Prepare the Elm web client for end-to-end encryption (E2EE) by creating a message rendering abstraction to handle encrypted and decrypted payloads, designing a message format with an encrypted_content field, and building infrastructure stubs for Signal Protocol integration, key management, and client-side decryption.
tasks.details: Begin by extending the Elm message model (from Task 5's state management) to include an encryption state, such as a union type like EncryptionState (Plaintext, Encrypted { encryptedContent : String, decryptionStatus : DecryptionStatus }, Decrypting, Decrypted { decryptedContent : String }). Design the message format to support an optional encrypted_content field in JSON decoders/encoders, ensuring backward compatibility with existing plaintext messages. Create a message rendering abstraction module (e.g., MessageRenderer.elm) that takes a message and renders it based on its encryption state: for plaintext, render normally; for encrypted, show a placeholder UI like 'Encrypted message - click to decrypt' with an indicator icon (e.g., a lock icon from an icon library or SVG). Implement a decryption hook interface as an Elm port or function stub that can be called to trigger decryption, preparing for future Signal Protocol integration by defining types for keys, sessions, and protocols (e.g., KeyBundle, Session, ProtocolVersion). Build key management infrastructure stubs, such as a KeyManager module with functions for storing/retrieving keys (initially using localStorage via ports, future-proofing for secure storage), and integrate with authentication from Task 2 for user-specific keys. Add encrypted message indicator icons to the UI, ensuring they are accessible and responsive. Document E2EE architecture decisions in a dedicated section of the project docs (e.g., README or architecture.md), covering choices like Signal Protocol for E2EE, client-side decryption flow (e.g., fetch keys, decrypt on-demand), and database schema considerations (e.g., storing encrypted_content as a blob, versioning for future-proofing). Prepare the client-side decryption flow by outlining the steps in code comments: receive encrypted message, check for decryption keys, prompt user if needed, decrypt using Signal Protocol stubs, update message state, and re-render. Future-proof database schema access by ensuring API clients (from Task 4) can handle the new encrypted_content field without breaking existing endpoints, and use Phoenix Channels (from Task 3) for real-time key distribution or message updates. Consider security implications, such as avoiding logging decrypted content and implementing rate limiting for decryption attempts. Use Elm's type system to enforce encryption states and prevent accidental exposure of plaintext.
tasks.testStrategy: Verify the message model extension by unit testing Elm decoders/encoders with elm-test, ensuring messages with encrypted_content parse correctly and fallback to plaintext for legacy messages; check that encryption state union types compile without errors. Test the message rendering abstraction by creating mock messages in different states (plaintext, encrypted, decrypted) and asserting the correct HTML output using elm-test or visual inspection in the browser, confirming placeholder UI appears for encrypted messages with indicator icons. Validate the decryption hook interface by simulating port calls (using Elm's test framework to mock ports) and verifying state updates upon 'decryption' (e.g., changing from Encrypted to Decrypted). Test key management stubs by mocking localStorage interactions and ensuring keys are stored/retrieved correctly without exposing sensitive data in logs. Confirm UI indicators by loading the app, sending/receiving mock encrypted messages via Phoenix Channels, and checking for lock icons in the message view using browser dev tools. Review documentation by cross-referencing architecture decisions against implementation, ensuring clarity for future Signal Protocol integration. Perform integration testing by simulating the decryption flow: inject an encrypted message, trigger the hook, mock successful decryption, and verify the message re-renders with decrypted content while maintaining performance (e.g., no UI freezes).

tasks.title: Elm Web Client: Deployment Pipeline & Rollout Plan
